lead: Steam tables and the Mollier chart are lookup tools. The tables list measured specific volume v (m³/kg), enthalpy h (kJ/kg) and entropy s (kJ/kg·K) for water and steam. They are arranged by pressure or by temperature; the dryness fraction is applied afterwards through the mixture formulas. The Mollier chart draws the same data on an h–s plane. Boiler designers, turbine testers and exam students use both to find all properties from a known pair. This chapter shows their layout and how to read a state.
prereq: You need: 5.1 for the five states of a pure substance, 5.3 for h_f, h_fg and dryness fraction, and Unit 1 for pressure units and gauge versus absolute pressure.

sections.h3: What the tables hold, and which pressure to use

blocks.text: A steam table lists measured properties of water and steam so one known property gives the rest. No single equation covers compressed liquid, wet steam and superheated steam accurately, so values are tabulated. Each row gives specific volume v in m³/kg, enthalpy h in kJ/kg and entropy s in kJ/kg·K.

Tables use absolute pressure. Absolute pressure is gauge pressure plus atmospheric pressure; atmospheric pressure is about 1.013 bar. A boiler gauge showing 10 bar means about 11.01 bar absolute, and 11 bar is what you look up.

blocks.where: p_abs is absolute pressure, p_gauge the gauge reading, p_atm the local atmospheric pressure (1.013 bar at sea level); all three in the same unit, bar or kPa.

blocks.text: The saturated table lists pressure with T_sat or temperature with p_sat. Both carry v_f, v_g, h_f, h_fg, h_g, s_f, s_fg, s_g. Subscript f marks saturated liquid, g saturated vapour, fg the change during boiling. So h_g = h_f + h_fg and s_fg = h_fg / T_sat, with T_sat in kelvin.
Inside the dome, pressure and temperature are not independent; a table row alone cannot fix the state. The dryness fraction x does: x = 0 is saturated liquid, x = 1 saturated vapour.
h = h_f + x·h_fg,   v = v_f + x(v_g − v_f),   s = s_f + x·s_fg
blocks.where: x is the dryness fraction (0 to 1); h_f and h_fg in kJ/kg; v_f and v_g in m³/kg; s_f and s_fg in kJ/kg·K. At low and moderate pressure v_f is far smaller than v_g (about 1/170 of v_g at 10 bar), so v ≈ x·v_g is used, except at very small dryness fractions where v_f must be kept.

blocks.text: Above T_sat the steam is superheated and the saturated table stops helping. The superheated table puts pressure down the rows and temperature across the columns. It has entries only where T is above T_sat at that pressure. Each cell gives v, h and s for that (p, T).

items: Look up T_sat at the given absolute pressure in the saturated table.
If T > T_sat, the state is superheated; open the superheated table.
If T = T_sat, the steam is saturated; use the saturated row with x.
If T < T_sat, the water is a compressed liquid; use the compressed liquid table, or h ≈ h_f at that temperature when pressure is small.
Find the pressure row, then the temperature column, and read v, h and s.

blocks.text: Printed tables jump in steps, often 50 K, so a given temperature may fall between two columns. Linear interpolation is accurate enough because each property varies smoothly with T at constant pressure.

blocks.where: y is the property wanted (h, v or s); (T₁, y₁) and (T₂, y₂) are the two table entries either side; T is the given temperature in °C.

blocks.text: Never interpolate across T_sat. Below saturation the temperature stays at T_sat while h climbs with x, so a formula built on T gives nonsense there.
Check: at 10 bar, h_g = 2777.1 kJ/kg, so any superheated h at 10 bar must be larger. A smaller answer means a wrong row or a gauge pressure.

The Mollier chart, also called the h-s diagram, plots enthalpy h in kJ/kg upward and entropy s in kJ/kg·K across. A state is one point and a process is a line, so you read with a ruler instead of a table.
The saturation dome sits in the middle. The left curve is saturated liquid (x = 0), the right curve is saturated vapour (x = 1), and they meet at the critical point near 221 bar and 374 °C.

items: Constant-pressure lines: inside the dome such a line is also a constant-temperature line, and it is straight, because at constant p the slope dh/ds equals T. In superheated steam the line curves upward and steepens as T rises along it.

Constant-temperature lines: inside the dome they coincide with the pressure lines. In superheated steam they slope gently upward to the right and become almost horizontal at low pressure, where steam behaves like an ideal gas and h depends on T alone. Near the saturation line at high pressure they rise much more steeply.
Constant-dryness lines: curves for x = 0.9, 0.95 and so on, fanning down from the critical point inside the dome; they place a wet state without a table.
For superheated steam, find the isobar for p and follow it to the isotherm for T.
Read h on the vertical scale and s on the horizontal scale.
For wet steam, cross the isobar inside the dome with the constant-x line.
Reject any point outside the dome that should have been inside it.

blocks.text: Reading a point on the printed chart is accurate to about 1 to 2 per cent. That is fine for a sketch or quick check; give final exam answers from the tables.

figure.caption: Given p and T, compare T with T_sat at that pressure to choose the table. The worked example takes the top branch: at 10 bar, T_sat = 179.9 °C, so steam at 250 °C is superheated.

spec.aria: A decision tree uses p and T to choose superheated steam, saturated steam or compressed liquid tables.

examples.question: Steam flows at 10 bar absolute and 250 °C. (a) State whether it is superheated, saturated or compressed liquid. (b) Here the superheated table for 10 bar gives entries at 200 °C and 300 °C: h = 2827.9 kJ/kg, v = 0.2060 m³/kg, s = 6.6940 kJ/kg·K at 200 °C, and h = 3051.6 kJ/kg, v = 0.2579 m³/kg, s = 7.1229 kJ/kg·K at 300 °C. Find h, v and s at 250 °C by interpolation.
steps: At 10 bar, T_sat = 179.9 °C. Given T = 250 °C > 179.9 °C, so the steam is superheated; the saturated table cannot give h, v or s.
Check: h_g at 10 bar is 2777.1 kJ/kg; 2939.75 is larger, so the state is superheated.
examples.answer: Superheated steam: h ≈ 2939.8 kJ/kg, v ≈ 0.2320 m³/kg, s ≈ 6.9085 kJ/kg·K. The tabulated value at 10 bar, 250 °C is about 2943 kJ/kg, so linear interpolation is within about 0.1 per cent.

traps: Entering the gauge pressure. At 10 bar gauge, absolute pressure is about 11.01 bar; properties read at 10 bar are wrong.
Using the saturated row when T > T_sat. At 10 bar and 250 °C, the saturated table gives h_g = 2777.1 kJ/kg, not 2939.8 kJ/kg.
Interpolating across T_sat, or writing the two temperatures in the wrong order so the correction changes sign.
Treating p and T as independent inside the dome. Wet steam at 10 bar is at 179.9 °C, whatever the question suggests.
Quoting the Mollier chart to three decimals. Reading a point is accurate to about 1 to 2 per cent, so use tables for final values and the chart for checks.

quiz.q: In a saturated steam table, what do the subscripts f, g and fg mean? Write the relation linking h_f, h_fg and h_g.
quiz.a: f = saturated liquid, g = saturated vapour, fg = change during boiling. h_g = h_f + h_fg.

quiz.q: A gauge on a steam line reads 10 bar. What absolute pressure goes into the table? Take atmospheric pressure as 1.013 bar.
quiz.a: p_abs = 10 + 1.013 = 11.013 bar, entered as about 11 bar.

quiz.q: Why does the superheated table have no entry for steam at 10 bar and 150 °C?
quiz.a: T_sat at 10 bar is 179.9 °C, so 150 °C lies below saturation. The water is a compressed liquid there, and superheated entries begin only above T_sat.

quiz.q: On an h-s chart, explain why a constant-pressure line inside the dome is also a constant-temperature line.
quiz.a: Inside the dome pressure and temperature are tied by saturation, so fixing p fixes T at T_sat. The slope dh/ds at constant p equals T, which is constant, so the line is straight.

quiz.q: Steam at 5 bar absolute has x = 0.9. Given h_f = 640.1 kJ/kg, h_fg = 2107.4 kJ/kg and v_g = 0.3749 m³/kg, find h and v.
Steam at 10 bar has s = 6.0000 kJ/kg·K. Using s_f = 2.1381 and s_fg = 4.4469 kJ/kg·K at 10 bar, find the dryness fraction.
A student reads the Mollier chart at 10 bar and 250 °C and gets h = 2890 kJ/kg, while the table gives 2939.8 kJ/kg. Which value should be trusted, and what could explain the gap?
quiz.a: The table, because it is the reference data. The gap is about 50 kJ/kg, roughly 1.7 per cent of 2940 kJ/kg, inside the chart's reading accuracy of about 1 to 2 per cent (2 per cent is about 59 kJ/kg). A gauge pressure used by mistake or a misread isotherm would add a larger error on top.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industrial steam properties now come from the IAPWS-IF97 formulation, equations fitted to laboratory data that reproduce printed tables to within a fraction of a per cent. Software such as CoolProp and REFPROP evaluates it directly, so design codes never interpolate by hand. The Mollier chart survives in plant rooms because a line shows a whole expansion at a glance. Search "IAPWS-IF97 steam tables" or "CoolProp water properties" to see the equations behind the printed rows.
